stories.title: You Have Died of Dysentery
stories.dek: The Oregon Trail disease is back, it’s an STI now, and the CDC filed it under food poisoning.
summary: Shigella, the bacterium that killed your pixelated ox-cart family on an Apple IIe in 1987, has spent the last decade reinventing itself as a sexually transmitted infection. The CDC’s own April report examined 16,788 samples: extensively drug-resistant cases, immune to all five oral antibiotics we would normally use, went from zero in 2011 to 280 in 2023, and more than a third of those patients were hospitalized. The treatment recommendation, quoted in full: there isn’t one.

How do you breed a superbug? A 2026 Lancet study calls it bystander resistance: you prescribe azithromycin for gonorrhea, and the shigella living in the same patient sits in on the course and graduates. We didn’t lose the fight to this bug. We trained it. And the agency responsible for noticing tracks it through its foodborne surveillance system, which is like tracking carjackings through the DMV.

stories.title: Trump Keeps Committing Treason Live On Camera
stories.dek: Article III defines exactly one crime. He is committing it on tape, to applause.
summary: Three times in three days, the president stood in front of a wall of American flags and invited a country we are at war with to hit two American cities. Monday in Grand Island: “Let ’em take out Los Angeles. Let ’em take out San Diego.” Wednesday in San Antonio: “I said it the other day: let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles.” He opened with “I said it the other day.” He knew, and he did it again as a callback. Comedians do callbacks. Presidents are not supposed to do them with the names of cities.

Thirteen million people live in those two counties, and San Diego is the home port of the Pacific Fleet, so the commander in chief invited an enemy to put a missile into his own ships. The Constitution defines exactly one crime. Article III, Section 3: adhering to their enemies, giving them aid and comfort. When Republicans on the ballot are breaking with you over which American cities you’d sacrifice, you have located a brand-new bottom.

stories.title: Trump Called Two American Cities a “Small Price.” Hurricane Isaias Would Like a F@#king Word.
stories.dek: Twenty-six days before the midterms, the Gulf is about to send Republicans an invoice. Some might call it karma, but lives are at stake.
summary: On Monday night in Grand Island, Nebraska, the president stood before a cheering crowd and offered up Los Angeles and San Diego as a “small price” for his war with Iran and what it has done to gas prices. The crowd cheered. The White House cleanup crew said he meant nuclear weapons, which he never mentioned. San Diego’s mayor answered for the 115,000 service members who live there: “We are not expendable.”

Four days later the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season is crossing a bathtub-warm Gulf toward the oil coast, twenty-six days before the midterms. The small price is about to get a lot bigger, at the pump and in the places that were never supposed to be collateral.

stories.title: Ottumwa, Iowa Invited Religious Freedom and Got Exactly What It Ordered
stories.dek: A Satanic invocation sent a pastor into curse control. The warning had already been delivered.
summary: On October 6 a former Ottumwa city council member delivered a Satanic invocation at a council meeting. A pastor named Rick Bick (really) demanded the city reverse the curse, and the mayor called for thirty seconds of silence. Municipal government briefly became The Exorcist, with Robert’s Rules of Order in full force.

The thing is, the council adopted its invocation policy on January 20, and it explicitly embraces other belief systems and the absence of belief, and forbids the city from preferring one faith. Those were the instructions, printed, adopted, by a vote. The surprise is roughly equivalent to opening a salad bar and discovering someone chose cauliflower.

stories.title: Irkutsk: The Silence Isn’t an Answer
stories.dek: Reports of a possible Russian lab incident have raised alarming questions. Here’s why I’m staying alert and keeping speculation in check.
summary: An October 7 morning update on what we can responsibly conclude about the reported incident at Russia’s Anti-Plague Institute when reliable information is scarce: the unanswered questions around a lab worker’s death, why the first account never sat right with me, and how the Soviet record of bioweapons research and official secrecy informs the worry without proving anything about this case.

The honest takeaway is that we are in a wait-and-see period. The basic facts, the pathogen, and whether anything spread remain unresolved. I weigh both the reassuring and the worrying readings of the quiet, question whether a reported second death was duplicate reporting, and close with a separate concern about Trump’s comments on Russell Vought and the coming election.

stories.title: The Irkutsk Mystery: What Is Russia Hiding?
stories.dek: A 28-year-old lab worker is dead, official reports vanished, and Moscow’s story keeps changing.
summary: A 28-year-old worker at Russia’s Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute fell critically ill and died after an alleged incident involving plague bacteria. Nearly 200 contacts were placed under observation, hospitals locked down, the security services got involved, and senior health officials flew in from Moscow. Then the story started disappearing: reports deleted, explanations changed, and an official insistence that there was no outbreak at all.

With Julie Roginsky and Michelle Kinney of the Mayday Network, I dig into the contradictions and the history Moscow would rather the world forget, from the Soviet bioweapons program and the 1979 Sverdlovsk anthrax disaster to today’s anti-plague labs, and ask why the response on the ground is so out of proportion to the benign explanation. Nobody knows yet what happened. That uncertainty is exactly why it deserves attention.

stories.title: Trump Renames Artificial Intelligence After the One Thing It Isn’t Yet
stories.dek: The executive order tells every federal agency to say “Super Intelligence,” then assigns someone to figure out what that means.
summary: At the UN General Assembly the president announced that artificial intelligence would henceforth be called “super intelligence” in every United States document, because “artificial” makes it “sound fake and it is not fake.” A week later, after lunch with a table of tech executives, he signed the executive order. Let’s be clear: it is artificial. That is the whole point of the word. People built it, in buildings, with money.

The best part is that “superintelligence” was already a word, and it means something specific: a machine smarter than every human at everything, the hypothetical finish line serious researchers argue about whether we survive. The order renames the technology after the one thing it isn’t yet, then assigns someone to figure out what that means.

stories.title: If I’d Known You Were Gonna Die, I Wouldn’t Have Baked You That Cake
stories.dek: It’s been 41 years since my dad died. When do I finally get to let go of this grief and anger?
summary: April 11, 1984, was my father’s forty-sixth birthday. My mother had just started her first job outside the house, so my sister and I, fourteen and eleven, had him to ourselves, and I decided I would bake him a cake. I had already learned, by disaster, that “from scratch” did not mean dumping things in a bowl and expecting a frosted cake to appear.

He read in the bedroom with the classical station on while we banged around the kitchen. I remember the cake. O, lord, how I remember the cake. Forty-one years on, I am still asking when I get to let go of the grief and the anger, and whether that is even how it works.

stories.title: Something About the Irkutsk Plague Story Doesn’t Add Up
stories.dek: The dead lab worker. The extraordinary containment response. The Kremlin’s silence. The more we learn, the stranger this gets.
summary: I woke up thinking about a question that has been staring at us from the beginning. If Daria Shipilova was a lab tech at a place called the Anti-Plague Institute and broke a tube in an accidental exposure, wouldn’t she, of all people, know that antibiotics in the first twenty-four hours were the difference between living and dying? And wouldn’t that building have them? Yesterday I wanted people informed. Today I am more skeptical, and in a strange way both more hopeful about good outcomes and more wary of a real crisis.

Julie Roginsky makes the case that this is less a problem of epidemiology than of Kremlinology, and Kevin Esvelt, who leads a biosecurity lab at MIT, has called the Irkutsk facility a weapons-lineage lab. What we have is a mystery with potentially civilization-level stakes, told by an unreliable narrator, in a place where no independent reporting can reach. My biggest hope is that I am completely wrong. My biggest fear is that the people who know are telling us to pay attention, and the wrong people are in charge.

stories.title: The Fed Is Hitting the Brakes. AI Is Flooring the Gas.
stories.dek: Higher rates are supposed to make borrowers flinch. Families are. Businesses are. But Big Tech is borrowing hundreds of billions to win the AI race, and taking whatever price the market gives them.
summary: In July I wrote about the Layer War, the split between the Builders pouring hundreds of billions into AI data centers and the Layerers betting that intelligence becomes a cheap commodity. Right now the Builders look like they’re winning, and they’re no longer paying cash. Morgan Stanley expects the six biggest hyperscalers to spend $785 billion this year and close to a trillion next year, much of it borrowed. One strategist called them “price takers”: they will pay whatever the market charges, because pausing the race feels fatal.

Then I come home to northeast Indiana, where a $250,000 house is still real and a mortgage just jumped to 7.28 percent. Higher rates are supposed to make everyone flinch together. That’s how the brakes work. When one borrower refuses to flinch, the price of money rises until everyone else steps aside. The brake still slows traffic. It just changes who gets rear-ended.

stories.title: Russia’s Anti-Plague Lab Had a Plague. Then Officials Refused to Say “Plague.”
stories.dek: Six days, a dead lab tech, two hundred people in quarantine, and not one official who will say the word.
summary: I tried to play this one straight, which for me is unusual. Annie Jacobsen’s Biological War: A Scenario builds a terrifying fiction out of pieces that have all happened separately. Then Russia ran its opening chapter as a live table read.

On September 25, a twenty-eight-year-old lab assistant at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute broke a tube of live bacteria. She was diagnosed with “severe pneumonia” and died. Nearly two hundred contacts went into quarantine, and the public learned about it from a regional website and a Telegram channel. One official wrote “plague,” then edited it to “may have.” It looks like ordinary, curable plague. What failed first wasn’t the lab or the antibiotics. It was the telling.

stories.title: Win the Senate, Lose the Court: The GOP’s Lame-Duck F@#k-You
stories.dek: Alito left the door open. Republicans have walked through that door before.
summary: Sam Alito told CBS he’s thinking about retirement “every term,” and added that it’s hard to predict what any president might do with a replacement. A justice who swears he’s above politics just admitted he’s reading the polls like a bookie.

Here’s the math. If Democrats take the Senate on November 3, the new majority isn’t sworn in until January 3. If Alito retires in the eight weeks in between, a defeated Republican majority gets one last shot to lock in a seat for thirty years. Anyone who thinks they wouldn’t dare should remember Merrick Garland’s 293 days, and Amy Coney Barrett’s confirmation eight days before an election. Mark the lame duck on your calendar like a court date.

stories.title: Trump Made a 13-Year-Old Be His Own Lawyer. It’s Exactly as F@#ked Up as It Sounds.
stories.dek: No lawyer, two bad choices, and a deportation order for a kid who told the judge, “I have no one.”
summary: A thirteen-year-old from Honduras named Angel stood before a federal immigration judge in Harlingen, Texas, with no lawyer and no adult in his corner. The government brought its attorney. The judge offered him a choice between voluntary departure and a removal order, a call grown adults with law degrees agonize over. He cried, “I have no one,” and was ordered deported.

Most Americans assume everyone in court gets a lawyer. That right covers criminal court, not immigration court, even for kids. Congress tried to patch the hole in 2008 with a bipartisan law signed by George W. Bush, and for years a federal legal-aid program got children representation. I explain how that help disappeared and who decided a middle schooler should argue his own case.

stories.title: The Right Just Discovered Tillamook’s Halal Cheese. They’re About 10 Years Late.
stories.dek: The cheese didn’t change. A vegetarian enzyme did its job in 2016, and America’s outrage machine just declared jihad on cheddar.
summary: The outrage machine discovered a little “Certified Halal” mark on Tillamook cheddar and lost its mind. Someone called it “Al-Qaeda cheese.” The terrifying truth: in 2016, Tillamook switched to a fermentation-made rennet to keep its cheese from tasting bitter, and that rennet happens to qualify as kosher and halal. That’s the jihad. A microbe did its job.

As a secular Jew who skipped his bar mitzvah on purpose, I can report that forty percent of America’s packaged food is kosher-certified, and not one bite has made me more Jewish. So welcome, Tillamook, to the Dumb Boycott Hall of Fame, alongside plain Starbucks cups, smashed Keurigs, burning Nikes, and machine-gunned Bud Light.

stories.title: The Day I Decided Not to Become a Jewish Warrior for Israel
stories.dek: Or, how I learned to stop conforming and think for myself.
summary: In 1982, three Israeli recruiters came to my Hebrew School and asked a roomful of twelve-year-olds to sign up for the IDF in exchange for a free trip and a cheap gold menorah. Everyone signed. I didn’t. That night my mother told the school exactly what she thought of anyone recruiting her son for anybody’s army.

This essay starts there and ends in Gaza. I say plainly that October 7 was a horror and that Israel had every right to defend itself, and then I say what I believe it did with the world’s goodwill instead. As a gay, half-Jewish American who has never felt that Israel was mine the way this country is, I can’t stay quiet about violence done in my people’s name. Silence is complicity, and these atrocities do not speak for us.

stories.title: Why We Must Stand with Our Trans Siblings and Call Out the Real Threat
stories.dek: No one left behind: Democrats and even some LGBTQIA+ people struggle to answer this question when the moral and political stand is crystal clear.
summary: A Democratic push poll called me about trans rights, and every answer it offered was so mealy-mouthed I wanted to throw my phone. I’m a gay man in his fifties living in a very red state, and I have watched my own community trade away trans protections for a promised seat at the table more times than I can count.

So here it is without hedging: trans people are human beings, not a debate. The attacks on their health care, their kids, and their bathrooms are cruelty and a smokescreen for a party that has stopped governing. You can’t both-sides human rights, and no one gets left behind. That’s the deal.

stories.title: NAZA Documentary: Gaza, Israel and the Question of War Crimes
stories.dek: What happens when Israeli soldiers describe civilian deaths as part of the targeting calculus in Gaza, and a government answers with outrage instead of evidence.
summary: I open this one with a challenge: read it with your mind as wide open as you can make it. My earlier essays on Gaza made some people lose their minds, and before anyone welcomes me to a position they think I just discovered, I was first in line to despise Netanyahu back in 1995.

NAZA, a documentary by two Jewish Israeli directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, won a special jury prize at Venice. It’s built on rooftop testimony from twenty-four Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers about how civilian deaths were factored into targeting. Within forty-eight hours, Israel’s culture minister vowed to strip the filmmakers of their citizenship. I ask what it means when a government answers testimony with outrage instead of evidence.

stories.title: I Chose the Door Myself
stories.dek: After two years rebuilding from a career rupture I didn’t choose, I’m stepping fully into the independent business I built.
summary: The last time I left a job, I didn’t choose it. It ended after twenty-five years, in a meeting I still don’t understand, and was followed by two years of applications into the void: too expensive, too experienced, too fifty-something for rooms I had once helped build.

This time I chose the door myself and walked through it with the lights on, on a date I picked, with the work handed off cleanly. I’m going independent. Over two years on the side, I built a peptide-science publication, this Substack, a publishing company, and a podcast with my oldest friend. Somewhere in there, I stopped being a guy between jobs and became a guy with a business.

stories.title: The Next Global Superpower Is Already Taking Shape
stories.dek: Canada, Europe, and Ukraine are building something much bigger than NATO.
summary: Here’s my prediction: the newest superpower of the twenty-first century will be Canada, the European Union, and Ukraine, bound together. It sounds wild until you line up the news. Mark Carney is exploring an associate membership in the EU, and the EU, never flexible about new members, is apparently open to it.

Days earlier, Carney and Zelenskyy signed a hundred-year deal to mass-produce Ukrainian battle drones in Canada, with Ukraine getting thirty percent of the output. Put Europe’s market, Canada’s resources and manufacturing, and Ukraine’s hard-won experience fighting a modern war together, and you get something capable of redrawing the map for the rest of the century.

stories.title: The Men Racing to Build Superintelligence Are Asking Washington to Slow Them Down
stories.dek: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei says the AI race is moving too fast. OpenAI’s Sam Altman agrees. When the two biggest rivals in AI start asking for restraints, we should pay attention.
summary: One Saturday morning, Dario Amodei published 3,800 words asking the government to regulate his own company, and by lunch Sam Altman, his rival of four years, agreed. It’s easy to file that under corporate responsibility. Don’t. It isn’t a safety pledge. It’s a request for permission to stop, addressed to the only party that can grant it.

Amodei can’t be the only one who slows down, so he asked to be forced, including coordination among labs that antitrust law currently forbids. The two men are signaling to each other in public: if you back away from the gun, we will. I ask what they see that frightens them, and why the people closest to the models are the most afraid.

stories.title: Calculating Your Impending P(doom)
stories.dek: The people building AI have a number for the odds it ends humanity. They say it out loud, over salad. This week one of them quit and said it in public.
summary: Inside the AI labs, people casually trade a number: their p(doom), the odds that what they’re building ends humanity. When Jacob Coxon walked away from Anthropic and his stock options to say publicly that no frontier lab is acting responsibly, colleagues lined up behind him within the hour.

I start from the premise that AI is real and could be miraculous, which is exactly why the race worries me. It isn’t being built in a careful government lab. It’s being built by a handful of very rich companies sprinting to self-improving superintelligence, because the first one wins everything. The people closest to it think the odds are bad, and the stakes are only our entire civilization.

stories.title: Sugar Is Beating the Stock Market
stories.dek: The hottest asset in America is a commodity the government will not permit to have a price.
summary: Sugar is up about twenty percent this year, outrunning the S&P 500 and the entire AI trade, and Wall Street is treating it with a straight face. So naturally I launched a fund. Confectioners Alpha is structurally short Halloween, and its beet analyst has developed a tremor.

Under the satire is a real scandal. There is no free market for sugar in the United States, and there hasn’t been in my lifetime. Washington reserves most of the market for domestic growers, both parties protect the arrangement, and a few families collect. Randolph and Mortimer Duke needed a stolen crop report to rig orange juice for one morning. The sugar barons just needed a farm bill.

stories.title: A Legion of Children Before the Civil War
stories.dek: From Elon Musk? Ew, no. Just … ewwww.
summary: According to Ashley St. Clair, the richest man alive texted her that he needed “a legion of children before the civil war.” Not before the election. Before the civil war. The line surfaced in Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary Musk, and it should rearrange your afternoon.

I pull apart the public version of Musk’s birth-rate panic from the private one. One is a demographic worry repeated by credulous podcasters. The other is a man who expects the country to break into open violence and wants numbers on his side when it does. And of every word he could have chosen, he picked the one a demon uses in the Gospel of Mark.

stories.title: Eight Reasons Work in America Is a Disgrace This Labor Day
stories.dek: The idea was beautiful in 1882. By 1894 the president had signed the holiday and the deployment order in the same week.
summary: Labor Day began as something beautiful: in 1882, New Yorkers climbed lamp posts to watch working people march for a shorter day. Twelve years later, Grover Cleveland signed the federal holiday in the middle of the Pullman Strike and sent troops into Chicago five days later.

From there I count eight reasons work in this country is a disgrace, with receipts: real wages falling for months while corporate profits hit a record, a federal minimum wage frozen since 2009, health premiums rising like a second rent, and more. The money didn’t vanish. It moved, and it didn’t move to you.

stories.title: Nine Things I Wish Some Old Queer Had Told Me Before I F@#ked It All Up
stories.dek: Including the boring ones about paperwork, which are the ones that will actually save you.
summary: My generation came up without elders. They didn’t refuse the job. They died before they could do it. By 1994, AIDS was the leading cause of death for every American aged twenty-five to forty-four, and the men who should have taught me how to be forty never got to be thirty-five. So nobody wrote me this letter. I’ve been reverse-engineering it for thirty years.

Here are nine things for whoever is twenty-two right now and doing this without a map. Find old queers in person, on purpose. Come out on your own schedule. Get a doctor who doesn’t flinch. And do the paperwork: the will, the proxy, the beneficiary lines. It’s the least romantic advice on the list, and my generation paid for it in hospital hallways.

stories.title: The Best Numbers Since 2008, and Not One Point of Love
stories.dek: Democrats are up ten in party identification. Their own voters describe them in one word: weak.
summary: The good news: Democrats hold their widest party-identification lead in Gallup’s numbers since 2008, forty-nine to thirty-nine. The bad news: not one point of it is affection. The party is underwater on favorability, and when pollsters asked Democrats to describe their own party in their own words, the word that kept coming back was “weak.”

Voters aren’t choosing Democrats. They’re evacuating Republicans. I walk through what that means, why younger voters are drifting to independent, and what the party should actually do with a lead that’s on loan: show up, fund the races it has written off, and find a spine. Voters will hand Democrats a restraining order against the other guy, and those expire.

stories.title: 10 Ways Men Can Actually Honor Gloria Steinem
stories.dek: She didn’t want a black-and-white photo with the word “icon” under it. She wanted the dishwasher unloaded.
summary: When Gloria Steinem died at ninety-two, the men’s tributes all looked the same: a black-and-white photo, the word “icon,” and zero verbs. Reverence costs a man nothing. She had no use for it anyway. “Don’t agonize,” she said. “Organize.”

So here are ten things men can actually do, from saying the word “feminist” out loud where it costs something, to giving women the credit in the meeting, to raising our sons the way we’ve learned to raise our daughters. My generation had the curriculum on a record album by 1974. We’ve had fifty-two years to get around to it.

stories.title: The Bond Market Just Looked at America and Said, “Nah”
stories.dek: Global yields are exploding, AI is running on borrowed money, and the president who demanded lower rates may have just hired the guy who raises them.
summary: Every government bond market on Earth is lurching at once, and the years these yields last touched were each the year before something blew up. I lay out who lit the match: forty trillion dollars of debt, tariffs, and a shooting war that has oil climbing, all of it inflationary.

Then comes the punch line. Trump picked Kevin Warsh to cut rates, and Warsh walked into Jackson Hole talking like a man about to raise them. Meanwhile the AI boom holding the economy up is borrowing against buildings that don’t exist yet. I lived through 2000 and 2008. The bond market isn’t panicking. It’s doing math. The panicking is our job.

stories.title: They Threw Our Trans Siblings Overboard. Again. F@#k That.
stories.dek: Log Cabin Republicans drop the T—and audition for a lifeboat that was never coming for them.
summary: The Log Cabin Republicans voted to drop transgender people from their mission, in the same month the federal government started stripping trans people from their passports. The organization was born to fight a purge of gay teachers in 1978. Now it has looked at the people being purged today and pulled up the ladder.

I’ve watched this experiment before. In 2007, gender identity was cut from ENDA to make the bill “winnable,” and it protected no one. Throwing your trans siblings off the sled has never once slowed the wolves. The people who carried us through the worst years didn’t check whether we were respectable first. That’s what queer means to me, and these men aren’t it.

stories.title: Dolly Left Us One Last Song and We Can’t F@#king Have It
stories.dek: Filed under grievances we will be keeping until 2045. And under love. Mostly under love.
summary: The Gay High Council would like to lodge a formal complaint, through tears. Dolly Parton is gone, and somewhere in Pigeon Forge a finished Dolly song sits sealed in a time capsule until 2045. She told everyone it was really good. She also said, “I don’t know whose damn idea that was.” Dolly, honey. It was yours.

Then the reverence, which is most of this piece: what she was to queer people, from losing her own look-alike contest to a drag queen to never once flinching when loving us out loud cost something. Grief usually means there’s nothing left to wait for. She fixed that in advance, the way she did everything.

stories.title: COWARDS
stories.dek: The war on women is the war on democracy. Pick up a weapon.
summary: This is the most personal case I’ve ever made in print. It starts with something that happened to me when I was eight years old, and with what it taught me about men who feel entitled to smaller bodies and a civilization prepared to look away.

From there I lay out the war on women count by count: the predator class that keeps producing new names, the legislatures and courts grinding away at women’s autonomy, and the online pipeline radicalizing boys. Women have been fighting this war alone for long enough. The men who stay quiet are the cowards in the title. What side are you on?

stories.title: You Can’t Opt Out of AI. You Never Could.
stories.dek: The exit door is painted on. What I found when I went looking for a way out of the machine.
summary: At dinner, a friend I admire said quietly that she doesn’t use AI at all, and the table murmured its approval. I said nothing. I had more reason than anyone there to want her to be right: this technology pushed me out of a twenty-five-year career, and I’ve been rebuilding my life by becoming the thing that pushed me.

So I went looking for the exit, starting with an ordinary Tuesday. Her weather, her inbox, her coffee purchase, and her drive to work were all run through machine-learning models before she ever chose anything. The door out is painted on. The real questions are who controls the machine and who lives at the bottom of the hill it runs down.

stories.title: Power Comes First
stories.dek: Rewiring the Republic, Column Zero: the strongest case against this entire series, and why I am writing it anyway.
summary: In 2018, nearly two-thirds of Florida voters restored the franchise to 1.4 million people with felony records. Seven months later, the legislature took it back from about 774,000 of them with an invoice. The reform passed. The reform lost. The gap between those two sentences is what my series Rewiring the Republic is about.

This column makes the strongest case against the whole project: that reform lists are wish lists, and that nothing on them happens without power. I agree, and I’m writing the series anyway. Every one of the forty-three reforms gets an honest scorecard, including the box the wish lists skip: what breaks it. Every rung on the ladder is copper until someone throws the switch.

stories.title: The Guardrails Were Us
stories.dek: Rewiring the Republic, the Foreword: the repairs are not optional, and it has been done before, in worse weather than this.
summary: In one night in January 2025, seventeen inspectors general were fired, most by a two-line email, in plain violation of a law requiring thirty days’ notice to Congress. Nothing happened. The law was still on the books the next morning, fully in force and fully irrelevant.

I grew up believing American democracy was full of guardrails. It turns out most of them were norms, held up only because everyone agreed to behave as if they were walls. The guardrails were us. That can read as despair or as an assignment, and I choose assignment. The people who rewired this house before us weren’t braver. They were just earlier.

stories.title: The Layer War
stories.dek: China just made the model a commodity. Satya Nadella saw it coming, Apple bet the company on it, and the bill lands on people who were never in the room. Us.
summary: On a Thursday in July, a Beijing lab most Americans had never heard of released Kimi K3, a model that matched or beat America’s best on the work companies actually pay for, at half the price. Then it promised to give the thing away. Within a day, the chip index fell into a bear market, and the world’s most valuable company became Apple, the one that refused to build a frontier model at all.

This is the longest essay I’ve written, and it’s about the war underneath the melt: where AI’s money actually settles, who called it early (Satya Nadella did, in public), who bet catastrophically wrong, and who pays when the trillion-dollar promises come due. Someone always pays, and it is never the men in the room.

stories.title: The Wren in the House
stories.dek: Lindsey Graham is dead, and I don’t know what to do with that.
summary: I woke to a ransacked apartment, two cats in full predator mode, and a house wren that had come down the chimney overnight and survived until morning behind my bookcase. In old folklore, a bird in the house is a death omen, and a wren, the little king of the birds, foretells the death of a king. Then my phone lit up: Lindsey Graham had died overnight.

In the fable, the wren becomes king of the birds by hiding in the eagle’s feathers and fluttering out at the top. Graham spent forty years in the feathers of raptors, first John McCain and then a much bigger, much worse bird. I’ve tried all day to feel something clean about his death. This essay is about why I can’t.

stories.title: Your 2027 Grocery Bill Was Signed on June 29
stories.dek: The war, the tariffs, and the proclamation that set next year’s food prices, and the people who pay first.
summary: It opens in a combine cab outside Holdrege, Nebraska, in October. A fifty-eight-year-old farmer is bringing in a crop that is mostly not there, with an empty seat beside him where the man who rode that cab for nine years sat until he was taken in a July raid. Fertilizer he couldn’t afford, the most expensive diesel of his life, a drought, a steer sold early because hay cost more than the animal.

He could have survived any one of them. A farm isn’t built to take all of them at once. Then I follow the bill back to its source: a war that sealed the Strait of Hormuz, tariffs on every input a farm needs, and a June 29 proclamation that quietly admitted the emergency. You’ll be told nobody did this. It was one man, and the bill lands on the people with the least room, then on your grocery receipt.

stories.title: The Red Shard & The Pearl
stories.dek: Speculative fiction from a united Jerusalem, fifteen years after the seam was drawn in gold.
summary: This is a story from The Near Field, my series of speculative fiction that reaches a short way forward from what I’m thinking about now. It’s spring 2046 in a united Jerusalem. The schools let out early so the kids can half-watch an old man give a speech to two parliaments seated under one roof, and they find it about as thrilling as a recycling calendar. That boredom is the victory.

In the square, two rabbis and two imams argue, not about God, which they settled years ago, but about falafel. It’s a deliberately hopeful afternoon in a future that isn’t promised, offered not as a prediction but as a portrait of what we could still choose together.

stories.title: We Believe Everyone. Except the Jews.
stories.dek: Someone told me I warn about antisemitism because I’m paid to. That’s not an argument. It’s the oldest trope there is, and it’s how the wedge goes in.
summary: Someone suggested online that I write about rising antisemitism because I’m paid to. A person who believes he’s one of the good guys reached for the oldest slander in the Western canon, the Jew whose words are bought, and aimed it at a Jew warning about antisemitism. The insult demonstrated the thing it was meant to dismiss.

So here are my receipts. I’ve called what Netanyahu is doing in Gaza a genocide, in print, during the High Holidays. I’ve defended trans people, women, and Black officials in the same breath as Jews, because it’s always “all of us,” never “us alone.” If someone were paying me to shield Israel, it would be the worst-managed bribe in history. What’s left is the trope, and how it splits a coalition at the worst possible time.

stories.title: Rise Up, Corporate America!
stories.dek: Introducing fiduciary patriotism: if you want a thriving economy, you need a functioning democracy.
summary: Corporate America insists it’s a person, so I’m talking to it person to person. You spent the last decade optimizing for quarterly profits while tolerating a man who now threatens the stability your entire business model depends on: trade wars on a whim, retribution, attacks on the Constitution itself.

My argument is simple and very capitalist. Authoritarianism is incompatible with consumer capitalism. Frightened people don’t spend, uncertain people don’t invest, and nobody upgrades a phone in a surveillance state. If you are the citizens you claim to be, fiduciary duty now means defending democracy. There is no economy without it.

stories.title: I Love You, Dieter Murphy
stories.dek: The future is doomed, with me or without me. But me and Dieter Murphy, we’re going dancing.
summary: This is a short story. A time traveler from a fascist future lands in a sweltering Fort Lauderdale hospital in November 1989 with seventy-seven minutes, a silver ring, and an assignment: find his first boss, dying on an AIDS ward, and kill him on camera to buy his own freedom.

It’s a story about the men we lost, the friends we were too scared to say goodbye to at nineteen, and what you would do with one more hour if you could go back. I wrote it for the guardian angels of my generation. You’ll understand the title by the end.

stories.title: A Gun Virgin No More
stories.dek: This “gun control” liberal fires his first weapon.
summary: On a cold day in northern Indiana, a lifelong gun-control advocate fired an AR-style rifle for the first time, hit the target three times out of three, and called his best friend breathless. When she asked whether people should own these guns, the answer I’d given my whole life wouldn’t come out. I said, “I don’t know.”

This is me thinking out loud about why. Officeholders, soldiers, and new citizens all swear an oath to defend the Constitution against all enemies, foreign and domestic. Most of us born here never have. I’m not telling anyone to arm up. I am asking what we owe the Constitution when the people sworn to defend it won’t.

stories.title: Current Events Are Killing My Novel
stories.dek: Time keeps on slipping into the future …
summary: For eight years I’ve been building a science fiction trilogy set in 2042, after a Second Civil War and a Greater Depression broke North America into new nations. I made maps. I made flags. At the time, it all seemed far-fetched. Then the actual timeline started outrunning my plot.

This is a writer’s lament, with an excerpt about the Flash, the bomb that wipes out Washington in my book’s backstory. In the scheme of what we’re all facing, my distress ranks somewhere around billionth place. But I’m still writing, because the book is ultimately about hope, and about how science can help rebuild a shattered world.

stories.title: We’re Already at War
stories.dek: Welcome to the Reality War: a civil war and a world war, all in one.
summary: When Zelenskyy warned that cutting off aid to Ukraine could drag America and Europe into World War III, I didn’t feel shock. I felt vindication. My alarms had been screaming for months. Then I sat with my eighty-three-year-old mother, who depends on Social Security, as she asked how worried she should be about Musk’s crew inside government systems.

My generation grew up with The Day After and the mushroom cloud waiting in our future. The war came anyway, just in a new form: disinformation and the bending of reality itself. We lost the first battle without knowing we were in it. Facing that is the first step. Then we organize, and we try to be the light in the darkness together.

stories.title: In Between
stories.dek: A gay, half-Jewish Gen Xer tries to go home.
summary: I couldn’t get Linkin Park’s “In Between” out of my head, and for good reason. I had just moved back to Indiana after thirty years on the West Coast, to be near my aging mother, in the middle of my second divorce, after seven months of looking for work in the only career I’d ever had.

The country was in its own in-between, an interregnum between the old world and whatever clown car is coming next. Like Dante, I found myself in a dark forest with the straight way lost. This short piece is where I stopped apologizing for being in between, and started writing it down.
